output.title: Requirement freeze should be a control, not a prison
output.body:
If you run a small business, requirement freeze is useful only when the workflow still matches reality. The trouble starts when the process changes after it was written down: a repeat task needs exceptions, but the SOP or automation still assumes the old rule. At that point, the decision is not “AI or no AI.” It is more ordinary: keep the frozen spec and handle exceptions manually, update the spec and rebuild the workflow, or design the system to flag exceptions for human review. That last option is a design choice to scope in the diagnostic, not a claim that the system can decide for itself.

Bareni’s diagnostic approach fits that kind of decision. Identify one recurring workflow, be honest about whether AI fits, and define scope and measures before anything is built. For a founder, the useful threshold is the point where exception handling is no longer rare enough to ignore. If you are spending more time on exceptions than the workflow was designed to absorb, the frozen requirement is no longer protecting you; it is hiding the gap between the process on paper and the process in real life.

Practical next step: pick one documented workflow and ask, “What has changed since we froze this, and how many exceptions did I make this week?” If the answer keeps growing, the spec may be frozen in the wrong place. Human approval still owns any scope change, especially where money or other high-risk decisions are involved.
